Learning Objectives
Identify the epidemiology/risk factors associated with total knee arthroplasty for the
management of posttraumatic arthritis of the knee.
Evaluate a patient with posttraumatic knee arthritis.
Understand considerations specific to the surgical management of posttraumatic arthritis of
the knee.
Recognize common complications and their rates after total knee arthroplasty for the
management of posttraumatic arthritis of the knee.
Describe expected outcomes of total knee arthroplasty for the management of posttraumatic
arthritis of the knee.

Overview
Intra-articular fractures of the distal femur, proximal tibia, or patella may predispose patients
to posttraumatic arthritis later in life.
Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) in patients with posttraumatic arthritis may be complex because
of bone loss, ligamentous instability, and intra- and extra-articular deformities and soft-tissue
contractures.
Thorough evaluation and planning and knowledge and experience in the use of modular
revision knee systems are essential to achieving good clinical outcomes. Surgeons should
prepare for the need for additional fixation (stems and metaphyseal cones/sleeves) and
increased constraint during knee balancing.
In general, patients with posttraumatic arthritis who undergo TKA have higher complication
rates and poorer outcome scores than patients who undergo TKA for the management of
primary osteoarthritis.

Overview
Intra-articular fractures of the distal femur and the proximal tibia may predispose
patients to degenerative knee disease at higher rates than the general population. In
patients with posttraumatic arthritis, TKA can provide patients pain relief and
improvement in function. However, TKA may be complex in patients with posttraumatic
arthritis because of soft-tissue challenges (eg, previous incisions, previous flap or skin
graft coverage), bone loss, ligamentous instability, retained hardware, and intra- and
extra-articular deformity. Despite thorough evaluation and planning, the outcomes of
patients who undergo TKA for the management of posttraumatic arthritis generally are
inferior to those of patients who undergo TKA for the management of primary
osteoarthritis of the knee
Epidemiology/Risk Factors
Posttraumatic etiology constitutes 12% of symptomatic knee arthritis.
On average, posttraumatic arthritis presents in patients 9 to 14 years younger than primary
osteoarthritis.


Epidemiology/Risk Factors
Posttraumatic arthritis of the knee accounts for 12% of symptomatic knee arthritis.
Posttraumatic arthritis affects approximately 5.6 million people in the United States.
Symptomatic arthritis develops in 23% to 36% of patients after intra-articular knee
fracture, and this percentage seems unchanged with time.1,2 However, an increasing
disease incidence in the US military has occurred in the past two decades.3 These
patients are more active and have higher demands, presenting a mean of 9 to14 years
earlier than patients with primary osteoarthritis.4
In patients older than 40 years who sustain an intra-articular fracture about the knee,
3.3% are converted to TKA within 5 years5,6 (Figure 1). However, patients with a tibial
plateau fracture seem to be more likely to require later TKA than patients with a distal
femur fracture. In general, patients with a tibial plateau fracture are 5.3 times more likely
to undergo TKA than matched controls.7 However, French data show that the time from
trauma to TKA is a mean of 21.8 years (range, 1 to 56 years), indicating that a greater
proportion of these patients may eventually require TKA.8

Patient History and Physical Examination
The mechanism and date of injury and the dates and types of subsequent surgical
procedures should be documented. Previous complications, including infection and
venous thromboembolism, should be documented. Current function, including ROM,
instability, and pain, must be understood. The location of previous incision(s) should be
identified. Erythema, swelling, or drainage should be noted. Deformity should be
assessed regarding the coronal plane, length, and rotation in supine and weight-bearing
conditions. Finally, a careful neurovascular examination should be performed. If a
patient’s vascular status or soft-tissue flaps appear concerning, preoperative vascular
surgery and plastic surgery consultations are warranted.


Imaging Studies
Complete knee radiographs (ie, AP, lateral, Merchant/sunrise views) and weight-bearing
radiographs of the entire lower extremities should be obtained. For patients with
complex deformities involving rotational malalignment or considerable bone loss, CT can
be performed to better evaluate these conditions. Finally, angiography should be
performed in patients with severe defects and patients with an abnormal neurovascular
examination.
Serology
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level, white blood cell (WBC) count
If suspicious for infection, aspiration with synovial fluid cell count and differential count (WBC
count and neutrophil percentage) and culture

Serology
If infection is suspected, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level, and
WBC count should be obtained. In patients with high concern for infection, synovial fluid
can be obtained via aspiration and sent for synovial WBC count with differential and
culture. Newer tests, such as alpha-defensin and synovial C-reactive protein tests, also
can be performed to aid in the evaluation of infection.

Should be performed by an arthroplasty surgeon with access to a full catalog of implants with
stems, augments, cones, and increased levels of constraint (including rotating hinges;


Previous Hardware
TKA in patients with posttraumatic arthritis may involve complex reconstruction and,
therefore, should be performed by an arthroplasty surgeon who is familiar with and has
access to a full catalog of implants with stems, augments, cones, and rotating-hinge and
modular replacement systems.10 The Anderson Orthopaedic Research Institute
classification can be used to help define bone loss and indicate appropriate implant
choices.11
In many patients, previous hardware must be addressed. This can be done during the
same procedure as TKA or in a staged fashion. During single-stage hardware removal,
hardware should be removed through the incision through which TKA is performed or
should be able to be removed relatively percutaneously. Alternatively, the minimal
amount of hardware required to insert a TKA implant can be removed with the use of
metal-cutting burrs.
If hardware removal requires separate incisions or extensive dissection, staging
hardware removal and TKA is recommended. If hardware removal is performed in a
staged fashion, the hardware should be cultured, and incisions should be allowed to fully
heal (≥3 months) before TKA. Staging the procedure may decrease the infection rate;
however, no studies have been performed specifically on this subject.
In general, nails and plates in well-aligned limbs can be left in place (Figure 3). No
adverse outcomes have been demonstrated if tibial nails are left in place in patients
undergoing TKA.12 Computer-assisted navigation can be used in lieu of intramedullary
guides in the femur, allowing plates and nails to be left in situ without any difference in
outcomes compared with primary osteoarthritis cohorts.13,14

Deformity
Careful evaluation of deformity in the coronal, sagittal, and axial planes is essential. In
general, entirely intra-articular deformities can be managed via TKA alone. Appropriate
implants that can manage bone loss and ligamentous instability and provide additional
fixation must be available in those scenarios. The use of constrained implants is more
common after multiligamentous soft-tissue and bony injuries and demonstrates good
midterm survivorship in patients who undergo TKA for the management of
posttraumatic arthritis.15,16 Patients undergoing TKA for the management of

10.5), with no difference in survivorship compared with controls.17
In reconstructing bone defects, cement and screw rebar techniques are appropriate for
the management of defects smaller than 5 mm.18 For larger defects, metal augments
have proved vastly superior to cement and screw constructs and structural allograft.19-26
Cones and metaphyseal sleeves have proved durable in the management of large bone
defects, with nearly 100% survivorship in the posttraumatic setting27-29 (Figure 4).
Considerable bone loss and ligamentous instability can be managed well with the use of
constrained implants.30 However, increased surgical time is required if using these
modular systems.31,32

Early studies reported high rates of complications.
Most common complications include stiffness, wound healing, and periprosthetic joint
infection (PJI).

Complications
Patients undergoing TKA for posttraumatic arthritis have an increased risk of
complications compared with those undergoing TKA for osteoarthritis, and
approximately 90% of complications occur within 2 years postoperatively.38 Early studies
reported high complication rates, with stiffness, wound complications, and PJIs being the
most common complications.39–41 Interestingly, patella baja is an independent risk

More modern series continue to report an increased risk of complications and revision
surgery in patients with posttraumatic arthritis who undergo TKA.43,44 The overall risk of
revision surgery is approximately 1.5 to 2.5 times higher after TKA in patients with
posttraumatic arthritis compared with that after TKA in patients with osteoarthritis.45,46
The risk of PJI also is higher after TKA in patients with posttraumatic arthritis, with some
studies citing a more than threefold higher likelihood of infection in these patients.47-49
Stiffness, extensor mechanism complications, and wound problems also continue to be
more common after TKA in patients with posttraumatic arthritis.8,16,49 (Figure 6)


Surgical Outcomes
Historically, outcomes after TKA in patients with posttraumatic arthritis have been
inferior to those after TKA in patients with osteoarthritis. Higher rates of stiffness and
lower overall PRO scores have been reported in multiple studies, including a recent
meta-analysis50 (Table 1). Intra-articular deformities tend to be associated with better
outcomes, and previous soft-tissue injuries tend to be associated with better outcomes
than previous bony injuries.51,52 However, considerable improvements in PROs can be
expected after TKA in patients with posttraumatic arthritis, and patients with flexion of
less than 90° can expect improvement53,54 (Figure 7). However, recent studies from
high-volume institutions are challenging the previous paradigm and have demonstrated
no difference in PROs between patients with osteoarthritis and patients with
posttraumatic arthritis who undergo TKA.55,56

Pearls and Pitfalls
TKA may be complex in patents with posttraumatic arthritis, and a thorough patient history,
physical examination, imaging evaluation, and preoperative plan are essential.
The location of previous incisions and implants must be carefully evaluated. If previous
implants are removed during TKA, surgeons should remove only elements required to
appropriately position the TKA implant through the same incision or percutaneously. If
previous implants are removed in a staged fashion, surgeons should allow for complete
healing (≥3 months) of incisions before proceeding with TKA.
Availability of and familiarity with modular TKA systems that include metal augments, stems,
cones, and constraint options is required to adequately manage bone loss and ligamentous
instability.
Deformity can be corrected via TKA or in combination with osteotomy procedures,
simultaneously or in a staged fashion, depending on the location and degree of deformity.
Patients with posttraumatic arthritis who undergo TKA have a higher risk for complications,
including stiffness and PJI, and should be counseled appropriately.
Patients with posttraumatic arthritis can expect improvements in function, pain, and ROM
after TKA.
